title: Meta-analyses on charitable giving clarify evidence for empathic and effective altruism

paper_content.abstract:
Effective altruists argue that charitable giving is over-influenced by empathic responses and should
instead be guided by cost-benefit analyses about the effectiveness of giving. To provide insight into the
extent to which empathy and effectiveness are associated with charitable giving in the population, two
meta-analyses are conducted, synthesising 416 effect sizes from 124 papers sampling 74,797
participants. Here we show that effectiveness, r = .34, SE = .04, 95%CIs [.28, .40], and empathy, r =
.25, SE = .02, CIs [.21, .29], both positively relate to charitable giving overall. However, prediction
intervals reveal significant heterogeneity. Moderation analyses reveal one crucial caveat to the overall
association between effectiveness and charitable giving: although the mean effect is relatively large
when effectiveness is measured, r = .42, CIs [.35, .48], manipulated effectiveness has a weak effect, r =
.03, CIs [-.10, .17]. Our findings suggest that while people may self-perceive as effective altruists, they
give like empathic ones, a disjunction that calls for deeper causal investigation.
paper_content.introduction:
Understanding why and to what extent people engage in charitable giving has long been a
preoccupation of social scientists.1 One reason for this is that charitable giving serves an important
function in sustaining a healthy and inclusive society. Estimated at over $470 billion per year in the U.S.
alone2, charitable giving funds help, care, and services in ways that cannot be readily substituted
through commercial or government activities. As such, charitable giving is designed to enrich lives, and
in many cases to save lives. Another reason charitable giving has preoccupied scholars is its symbolic
value in signifying the degree to which people engage in kindness and compassion to others.
Understanding charitable giving helps us understand who we are as humans, and how we express our
humanity.

One of the biggest debates about charitable giving – both within and outside academia – is
whether people rely too much on their “heart” when giving, and not enough on their “head”. In his book
Against Empathy3 – and in high-profile opinion pieces4 – Paul Bloom makes the case that empathy is a
poor moral guide to charitable giving. In line with the empathy-altruism hypothesis5,6, Bloom agrees
that empathy plays a role in activating the motivation to do good. However, it also leads us to make
ineffective or unfair charitable decisions, focusing on issues that respond to our immediate emotional
triggers rather than grounding our compassion in rational deliberation about which causes do most good
(i.e., effectiveness considerations). Consistent with this notion, effective altruism scholars propose
decision-making frameworks for judging how effective one’s giving will be such as “How many people
benefit, and by how much?” and “What are the chances of success?”7-9 Although earlier critiques
positioned empathy and effectiveness as competing motives, recent evidence suggests they may be
mutually reinforcing, particularly when empathic concern is broadened to include distant others and is
guided by reasoning about impact.10-13

To assess research on the association between charitable giving, effectiveness, and empathy, a
key distinction lies between studies that rely on self-reports of these constructs and studies that
experimentally manipulated them. While the debate about the role of empathy in charitable giving has
gained increasing attention in recent years, prior syntheses have excluded experimental designs, making
this comparison unclear. When it comes to effectiveness, this distinction becomes especially salient
given high-profile experiments suggesting that donors have relatively little appetite to seek out
information about welfare impact14, and that when it is provided effectiveness information has limited
impact on charitable giving15 and choice of charities16.

The goal of this paper is to add an important missing piece to the debate: meta-analyses of the
extent to which charitable responses are, in fact, associated with empathy and perceived effectiveness.
By combining the voices of thousands of participants sampled by hundreds of researchers across several
decades, one is in a stronger position to distinguish signal from noise when examining the associations
between charitable giving, empathy, and effectiveness. We emphasise that the goal of this paper is not
to compare empathy and effectiveness directly. There are too few studies that measure both constructs
within the same sample, and the fields from which these constructs originate use different
operationalisations. Instead, our aim is to provide a descriptive and independent synthesis of the extent
to which each construct is associated with charitable giving, and under what conditions.

Before doing so, some definitional clarification is required. Empathy is a multi-dimensional
construct, one that is often used interchangeably with constructs such as sympathy and compassion. A
particularly important distinction is made between “emotional empathy”, which Bloom refers to as
“feeling what you believe other people feel – experiencing what they experience” (p.3)3 and “cognitive
empathy”, which is variously referred to in the literature as social intelligence, theory of mind, and
perspective taking. In Against Empathy, Bloom makes it clear that his case is primarily about the limits
of affective empathy. So although we meta-analyse all operationalisations of empathy here, we note that
it is affective empathy that is most closely aligned to the debate that inspired the current paper. As
illustrated below, empathy has been operationalised in many different ways (e.g., cognitive versus
affective; dispositional versus situational; experimentally versus correlationally) and drilling down into
the patterns for each helps illuminate the different ways in which empathy may be associated with
charitable giving. Empirical synthesis is overdue: the first meta-analysis on the link between empathy
and prosocial behaviour was published nearly 40 years ago, and incorporated only a handful of studies
on charitable giving.17 Subsequent syntheses have not examined experimental work, focusing
exclusively on correlational links between measures of empathy and questionnaire measures of
dispositional pro-social behaviour18,19 or between measures of empathy and resource allocations in lab-
based games such as the Dictator Game and the Prison er’s Dilemma20.

In extracting data for the effectiveness meta-analysis, we excluded the related literature on
efficiency, that is, the proportion of money that goes to beneficiaries as opposed to being absorbed by
administrative costs.21,22 We made this decision in line with the arguments of effective altruism
advocates, who make it clear that the efficiency of a charity should not be a primary criterion for
judging whether it is effective (i.e., a charity for which 99.99% of income is funnelled directly towards a
pointless mission is efficient but not effective)7. Instead, we meta-analyse studies that measure or
manipulate variables sometimes referred to as “response efficacy”, “perceived donation efficacy”, or
“perceived impact of donation”: constructs that are measured through items such as “How much good
do you think you can do by donating money to this organisation?” or “To what extent do you think that
your donation would make a positive difference?”

Finally, we restricted our analysis to charitable giving, as distinct from other forms of prosocial
behaviour. We defined charitable giving as “voluntary contributions of money that benefit people
outside the giver’s family”.1 We had two reasons for restricting the analysis to charitable giving. First, it
is an operationalisation of giving that most closely aligns to the effective altruism movement, which is
best known for providing moral context around which charities to support financially. Second, by
restricting the range to one domain of prosocial behaviour, we reduce statistical noise and unwanted
heterogeneity associated with comparing effect sizes across different behaviours.23 Patterns of altruism
across domains (e.g., donating money versus blood versus time) are psychologically distinct24, so
focusing just on charitable giving leaves us in a better position to make like-for-like comparisons
between studies.

Here, we show through two meta-analyses that empathy is a robust correlate of charitable giving
and reliably increases generosity when experimentally evoked. Perceived effectiveness, on the other,
hand predicts giving strongly at the self-report level and weakly under experimental manipulation. We
conclude that people give like empathic altruists even when they see themselves as effective ones, a
pattern that sharpens the empirical context within which debates about effective altruism unfold.
paper_content.results:
We followed the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-analyses
(PRISMA)25,26 to identify quantitative research on (1) the association between effectiveness and
charitable giving and (2) the association between empathy and charitable giving. PRISMA flowcharts,
summarising the screening process, are presented in Supplementary Figs. S1 and S2. Full reference lists
for papers included in the empathy and effectiveness meta-analyses are included in the Supplementary
file.

Pearson’s correlation (r) was used to represent the association between charitable giving and the
two variables of interest: effectiveness and empathy. To approximate a normal sampling distribution,
Pearson r correlations were transformed to Fisher’s z correlations for analyses. For ease of
interpretation, we report values transformed back to Pearson r correlations. Given that the majority of
articles included in both meta-analyses reported multiple dependent effect sizes, we employed a three-
level meta-analytic approach to calculate the overall effect size and perform moderator analyses. All
tests of significance are 2-tailed unless otherwise specified.

We examined publication bias in two ways: visual inspection of the Funnel Plots (where
asymmetry may indicate publication bias) and Egger’s Sandwich test, which was used given the
presence of dependent effect sizes. As can be seen in Fig. 1, no clear or systematic asymmetry is shown
for either meta-analysis. Consistent with visual inspection, Egger’s tests were non-significant for both
effectiveness (p = .260) and empathy (p = .804), indicating no statistical evidence of a pattern indicating
publication bias.

Heterogeneity and treatment of moderators.

We calculated I2 (the proportion of total variance in study results due to heterogeneity rather
than sampling error) which suggested a high degree of heterogeneity for both the effectiveness (96%)
and empathy (92%) meta-analysis. To determine if the within-paper variance (Level 2) and between-
paper variance (Level 3) were significant, two one-tailed log-likelihood-ratio tests were performed.
These tests compared the fit of the three-level model (which accounted for variance at Levels 2 and 3) to
the fit of a two-level model in which variance at only one of the levels was freely estimated. Significant
variance in effect sizes was observed at both the within-paper level (both ps < .001) and between-paper
level (both ps < .001). Using Cheung’s27 formula, 2.48% of the total variance in the association between
effectiveness and charitable giving, and 5.46% of the variance in the association between empathy and
charitable giving, was attributed to sampling variance. Considerably more variance is attributable to
within-paper variance (32.33% in the effectiveness analysis, 24.11% in the empathy meta-analysis) and
between-paper variance (65.19% for effectiveness, 70.43% for empathy). In addition to estimating the
overall effect size, we calculated the prediction interval for each meta-analysis. Prediction intervals
estimate the likely range of effect sizes that might be observed in future studies with similar
characteristics. The range of effect sizes was r = -.17 to r = .71 for effectiveness and r = -.14 and r = .57
for empathy. These heterogeneity tests indicate that the true effects vary significantly across papers and
measures, and that future studies on these associations may report correlations that vary widely.

Moderation analyses identify likely causes of this heterogeneity. To account for the potential
issue of multicollinearity, we followed Hox and colleagues’ recommendation to first test for the effect
of each potential moderator separately using univariate models.28 We then conducted multiple
moderator analyses on a single model that included all significant moderators identified in the univariate
analyses for each meta-analysis.

In the main body of this manuscript, we discuss moderators that are most relevant from a
theoretical and/or practical perspective. For the sake of thoroughness, however, we also ran ancillary
moderation analyses based on sample characteristics: the proportion of women in the sample; the
average age of participants; whether data were collected in Western, Educated, Industrialised, Rich, and
Democratic (WEIRD) or non-WEIRD countries29; whether the sample comprised students or non-
students; and whether the sample was collected using online or offline methods. These analyses are
reported in the bottom half of Tables 1 and 2. In short, none of these sampling characteristics were
statistically significant moderators of the association between effectiveness and charitable giving (all ps
> .35) or the association between empathy and charitable giving (all ps > .08) and so we do not
elaborate on these analyses further.

Effectiveness

Overall, a medium-sized positive association was found between effectiveness and charitable
giving, r = .34, p < .001, t = 9.85, 95% CIs[.28, .40]. However, as can be seen in Table 1, three
moderators significantly qualified this conclusion. First, the association was significantly stronger when
charitable giving was self-reported (e.g., willingness to donate, future intentions to donate, self-reported
past giving; r = .38, p < .001) than when studies used behavioural measures of giving (e.g., direct
observations of giving in the field, the amount of a study payment that the participant donated; r = .27, p
< .001). Second, the association was significantly stronger when participants reported their likelihood of
giving (r = .37, p < .001) compared to when participants reported a monetary value of giving (r = .29, p
< .001). Third, the association between effectiveness and charitable giving was only significant when
effectiveness was measured (r = .42, p < .001). When effectiveness was manipulated, the average effect
was trivial in size and statistically non-significant (r = .03, p = .612).

Finally, we examined whether the different operationalisations of effectiveness corresponded to
differences in strength of association. In the literature, the dominant operationalisation was what we
refer to here as donation effectiveness, a construct that is sometimes referred to as “response efficacy”,
“perceived donation efficacy”, or “perceived impact of donation”. What unites these operationalisations
is that they refer to the extent that the donation will be effective in achieving positive outcomes
(example item: “How much good do you think you can do by donating money to this organisation?”).
However, as can be seen in Table 1, at least three other operationalisations exist in the literature. What
we label as charity effectiveness refers to perceptions of the effectiveness of charities in general
(measured by items such as "Charitable organisations have been quite successful in helping the needy").
What we label as collective effectiveness refers to perceptions of the extent to which collectives can
make a difference (e.g., “I think together we can successfully change things in relation to this issue”)
whereas personal effectiveness refers to perceptions of whether participants can personally make a
difference (e.g., “I think it seems possible to make a big difference"). Regardless of how effectiveness
was operationalised, a significant and positive association was found, the strength of which did not
differ reliably across dimensions.

Following Hox and colleagues’ recommendations28, we extended the three-level meta-regression
model to simultaneously include the moderators identified to be significant in the univariate analyses
(i.e., measured vs manipulated, self-report vs behaviour, likelihood vs value). The multiple moderator
analysis was significant, F(3,150) = 15.51, p < .001, revealing a significant unique moderating effect of
measured vs manipulated effectiveness on the overall association between effectiveness and giving (see
Table 3 for number of effect sizes and statistical output).

Consistent with the univariate analyses, when effects of the other significant moderators were
taken into account, the association between effectiveness and charitable giving was again only
significant when effectiveness was measured (and not when effectiveness was manipulated). However,
the other moderators (self-report vs behaviour, likelihood vs value) were no longer significant. A
possible explanation is that these variables covaried with the measured versus manipulated distinction.
Specifically, experimental studies were more likely to employ behavioural outcomes (rather than self-
reports) and assess donation value (rather than likelihood), which may have suppressed the independent
contributions of these moderators in the full model. In this context, the available data make it difficult to
completely disentangle their unique effects within the multivariate analysis.

Empathy

Overall, a medium-sized positive association was found between empathy and charitable giving,
r = .25, p < .001, t = 11.55, 95% CIs[.21, .29]. Contrary to the pattern of the effectiveness meta-analysis,
there was no statistically significant difference in the strength of that association depending on whether
empathy was measured or manipulated (both rs = .25, both ps < .001; see Table 2). As in the
effectiveness meta-analysis, the association between empathy and charitable giving was significantly
stronger when giving was self-reported (r = .27, p < .001) than when studies used behavioural measures
of giving (r = .22, p < .001). The association was also significantly stronger when giving was measured
in terms of likelihood of giving (r = .29, p < .001) versus the monetary value that participants gave
(r=.21, p<.001). Moreover, a stronger association was found when empathy was operationalised
situationally (i.e., as a state variable; r = .27, p < .001) than when it was measured dispositionally (i.e.,
as a trait variable; r = .20, p < .001).

A final moderator was the dimension of empathy that was being captured. A common critique of
the field is that researchers’ use of the term “empathy” glosses over theoretically meaningful
distinctions. In our systematic review, the dominant operationalisation was what we label here as
emotional empathy, incorporating constructs united by a focus on emotion felt toward a group or
individual in need (variously described in the literature as “compassion”, “sympathy”, “empathic
concern”, or “affective empathy”). As can be seen in Table 2, the strongest association between
empathy and charitable giving emerged when empathy was operationalised this way (r = .27, p < .001).
Significantly weaker than this (but still significant; r = .20, p < .001) were effect sizes in studies in
which empathy was operationalised in a more cognitive way (e.g., as a form of perspective taking
toward a group or individual in need but without any reference to emotion). Finally, some studies
measured empathy as personal distress without explicitly linking that distress to a target group. Most of
these were drawn from studies using the personal distress sub-factor of the Interpersonal Reactivity
Index, which incorporates items such as “Being in a tense emotional situation scares me”.30 When
operationalised this way, empathy shared a relatively small association with charitable giving (r = .09, p
= .005), significantly weaker than for the other two dimensions.

We extended the three-level meta-regression model to simultaneously include the moderators
identified to be significant in the univariate analyses (i.e., state vs trait, dimension of empathy, self-
report vs behaviour, likelihood vs value). The multiple moderator analysis was significant, F(5,228) =
20.15, p < .001, revealing a significant unique moderating effect of state vs trait empathy, dimension of
empathy, and likelihood vs value on the overall association between empathy and giving (see Table 4
for number of effect sizes and statistical output).

When effects of the other significant moderators were accounted for, studies that measured state
empathy yielded a significantly stronger relation compared to studies that measured trait empathy.
Similarly, an identical pattern of findings to the univariate analyses emerged for the dimension of
empathy and likelihood vs value moderators: studies that measured emotional empathy and cognitive
empathy yielded a significantly stronger association than those that measured personal distress, and
studies that captured giving likelihood yielded a significantly stronger association compared to those
that captured giving value. In this model, however, the self-report vs behaviour moderator was no longer
significant.
paper_content.methods:
Search strategy

Literature searches were initially run in November 2019 and the search was refreshed in
December 2022. The search was conducted across four databases: the two largest multidisciplinary
academic databases (Scopus and Web of Science) plus content-relevant databases in business
(ABI/Inform) and psychology (PsycINFO). For both libraries we used search terms nested around
charitable giving (donation*, donate, donor*, philanthrop*, charitable, "not for profit*", "non profit*",
nonprofit*, NGO*, "non governmental", “third sector” , "charit*") and the factor of interest:
effectiveness (“effective altruism”, “effective giving”, "donation effective*”, “charity effective*”,
“nonprofit effective*”, efficacy, competence, "impact of gift", "donation impact", “nonprofit impact”,
“charity impact”), and empathy (empath*, sympath*, compassion*). Searches were based on title,
abstract, and keywords. Results were supplemented through snowballing from reference lists and open
calls for unpublished data distributed through X and mailing lists of the Association for Research on
Nonprofit Organizations and Voluntary Action, American Marketing Association, and Society for
Personality and Social Psychology. To help identify relevant grey literature, we also screened the first
20 pages (200 results) in Google Scholar (consistent with standard practice)42 using the same search
terms identified in the database searching.

Inclusion criteria and screening

To be eligible for inclusion, studies needed to include a quantitative measure of charitable giving
(as part of correlational or experimental designs), be reported in English, and published 1980 or later.
Correlational studies allowed us to estimate the strength of naturalistic associations, while experimental
studies enabled us to examine causal effects of manipulating empathy or effectiveness on giving
behaviour. We excluded purely qualitative, theoretical, or descriptive studies because they do not
provide effect sizes or statistical associations necessary for meta-analysis. Similarly, we did not include
studies based on simulation models, ethnographic observation, or administrative records without direct
measurement of the psychological constructs of interest, as these designs do not allow for computation
of comparable quantitative associations.

In these meta-analyses, we coded for several moderators. In doing so, we defined intention
likelihood as a self-reported assessment of the likelihood or willingness to donate to a charitable cause
(e.g., “How likely are you to donate to this organisation?”). Value was defined as the monetary value
participants reported they would donate or actually donated. We distinguished between measured
giving, where donation behaviours or intentions were assessed without experimental manipulation of the
constructs of interest, and manipulated giving, where donation behaviours or intentions were measured
after an experimental manipulation aimed at influencing empathy or perceived effectiveness. Self-report
measures refer to participants’ stated responses to survey items about their donation intentions or
behaviour (e.g., likelihood of donating or intended donation amount), whereas behavioural measures
involve participants making actual donation decisions, typically involving real or incentivised financial
contributions.

There were no limits on age or nationality of participants. Papers that were not full-length
articles (e.g., book reviews, books, conference abstracts, corrections, legal judgements) were not
included. The second and third authors screened texts for eligibility on title and then again on abstract,
resolving discrepancies through discussion. Both screeners had experience conducting and publishing
meta-analyses previously. Screening on the full text was conducted by the second author. For articles
less than 10 years old that did not report bivariate effect sizes, we emailed authors to request this
information.

Analytic strategy

Following the screening process, data on the association between effectiveness and charitable
giving were analysed from 47 papers, comprising 81 independent samples and 157 effect sizes (N =
32,116). Data on the association between empathy and charitable giving were analysed from 77 papers,
comprising 105 independent samples and 259 effect sizes (N = 42,681). Where an experiment both
manipulated and measured effectiveness (for example as a manipulation check) both effect sizes were
included (one in the “manipulated” category and one in the “measured” category).

We employed a three-level meta-analytic approach to calculate the overall effect size and
perform moderator analyses. To determine the appropriate level at which to model statistical
dependence among effect sizes, we compared alternative multilevel random-effects structures and
modelled dependence at the paper level; model comparisons and sensitivity analyses are reported in the
OSF supplement. The total variance is partitioned into three components: sampling variance (Level 1),
within-paper variance reflecting dependence among studies in the same article (Level 2), and between-
paper variance (Level 3), thereby appropriately accounting for the clustering of effect sizes. To conduct
our analyses, we followed the procedures outlined by Assink and Wibbelink43 and used the rma.mv
function of the Metafor package44 in the R environment (version 4.4.0)45. We used a multilevel random
effects model, and restricted maximum likelihood estimation method to calculate all model parameters.
The t-distribution was used to test individual regression coefficients and for calculating confidence
intervals46.

The type of bivariate effect size extracted depended on study design, but we typically extracted
Pearson’s correlation coefficients (r) for correlational studies or Cohen’s ds for experimental studies. In
situations where these values were not provided by the study, we used test statistics (e.g., means and
standard deviations, F-values, frequency data) to calculate effect sizes. All effect sizes were transformed
to Pearson r correlations for the meta-analysis (see OSF for effect size conversion formulas).

A leave-one-out analysis did not identify any studies that influenced the overall findings. To
check for extreme effect sizes that may disproportionately influence the results, we screened for those
with standardised scores larger than 3.29 or smaller than 3.29.47 No outliers were identified in the
effectiveness meta-analysis, and only one outlier was identified in the empathy meta-analysis.
Regardless of whether this effect size was included or excluded, analyses yielded similar findings, so we
opted to include this effect size in all subsequent analyses.

Data availability statement

The data are publicly available on the Open Science Framework:
https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/QZ9AX. 48

Code availability statement

Analyses were conducted through R, using code that is viewable on the Open Science Framework:
https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/QZ9AX. 48

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1: In a meta analyses of 416 effect sizes from 74,797 participants, the authors examine the extent by which charitable giving is shaped by perceptions of effectiveness versus empathy. They find that self-reported effectiveness perceptions explain more variance in charitable giving than empathy, but effectiveness interventions do not reliably influence charitable giving. This is my first time reviewing this paper. I appreciated the opportunity to read this work. The key strength of the paper is the inclusion of two large-scale meta-analyses aggregating an impressive number of studies on charitable giving, which provide a nuanced perspective about the extent to which empathy and effectiveness perceptions motivate charitable giving and confirm rather paradoxical behaviors that people self-report in ways that imply effectiveness is very important to them, but seem relatively unmoved by actual effectiveness information. With reasonable updates, I think this work will be of interest to a broad readership. These are the things I suggest to help make the paper stronger: MAJOR COMMENTS Empathic Versus Effectiveness Debate The introduction—notably the 2nd, 3rd, and 4th paragraphs—set up a debate about “empathic” versus “effective” altruism, but then state that the “goal of this paper is not to weigh up the moral arguments of the effective altruism movement or the case against empathy” but to conduct “meta-analyses of the extent to which people are, in fact, influenced by effectiveness and empathy in making charitable decisions” (pg 3). This was quite striking to me for several reasons. First, Bloom’s arguments are not that people do not engage in empathic charitable giving, but that it may be unfair or less effective at actually helping. Second, and more importantly, much work over the last decade suggests that empathic and effective altruism are more compatible than previously argued (e.g., Everett et al., 2018; Fowler et al., 2021; Law et al., 2022, 2024). Setting up this debate in order to ask “to what extent does empathy or effectiveness drive charitable giving?” seems misleading and distracting from the main study. An alternative motivation might be best described by the authors in the Discussion, which focus on the following questions: Is charitable giving overly influenced by empathy? Is charitable giving under-influenced by analytical, cost-benefit analyses about maximising good? How successful is empathy induction in promoting charitable giving? How successful are effectiveness interventions in promoting charitable giving? Readers may benefit more by motivating your study from this perspective and providing additional background on evidence for the "effectiveness paradox" rather than the empathy versus effectiveness debate. Everett, J. A., Faber, N. S., Savulescu, J., & Crockett, M. J. (2018). The costs of being consequentialist: Social inference from instrumental harm and impartial beneficence. Journal of Experimental Social Psychology, 79, 200-216. Fowler, Z., Law, K. F., & Gaesser, B. (2021). Against empathy bias: The moral value of equitable empathy. Psychological Science, 32(5), 766-779. Law, K. F., Amormino, P., Marsh, A. A., & O’Connor, B. B. (2024). Ethical reasoning versus empathic bias: A false dichotomy? Trends in Cognitive Sciences, 28(1), 1–4. Law, K. F., Campbell, D., & Gaesser, B. (2022). Biased benevolence: The perceived morality of effective altruism across social distance. Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin, 48(3), 426-444. Statistical Models It appears that the authors run separate models for empathy and effectiveness and then qualitatively compare the effect sizes from each of the models to draw their conclusions (e.g., that perceived effectiveness predicts charitable giving over and above empathy). Is there a way to statistically compare these effect sizes directly? The authors might be limited by having no or few studies that measure both empathy and effectiveness (were there any that measured both?), but comparing effect sizes would immensely improve the inferences drawn by the results. If not, then this should be noted as a limitation. Other Forms of Altruism The authors focus on charitable giving, a well-studied and valid form of altruistic giving. How do they speculate their findings generalizing to other forms of altruism, such as stem cell donation or organ donation? Interestingly, the results show that self-reports of empathy are robustly associated with charitable giving. How do the authors reconcile these findings which recent work finding that self-reports of empathic concern are not robust predictors of other forms of real-world altruism (Rhoads et al., 2023)? Do the authors believe there is something specific about the relationship between empathic motivation and acts of charitable giving—perhaps the relative cost of charitable donations is lower or perhaps acts of charity are more outward forms of social or moral signaling linked to social desirability biases or norms? Rhoads, S. A., Vekaria, K. M., O’Connell, K., Elizabeth, H. S., Rand, D. G., Kozak Williams, M. N., & Marsh, A. A. (2023). Unselfish traits and social decision-making patterns characterize six populations of real-world extraordinary altruists. Nature Communications, 14(1), 1807. Describing the Included Studies The authors need a table either in main text or supporting information describing the specific measures used in each of the studies included their analyses and how they were classified. I did not see any description of this and thus it was difficult for me to interpret any of the results. For example, what does “Behavioural” mean in Table 2? Which behavioural measures of giving were used? This practice is fairly standard in meta-analysis papers. MINOR COMMENTS Perceived Effectiveness: I suggest the author stick with the term “perceived effectiveness” when discussing self-report effectiveness but describe it earlier. Typo on Line 205: “r = .??, p = .??” Lines 91-93: The authors state “the last meta-analysis on the link between empathy and prosocial behaviour was published over 35 years ago, and incorporated only a handful of studies on charitable giving.” However, meta-analytic studies have investigated the relationship between empathy and prosociality since Eisenberg & Miller (1987), notably: Thielmann, I., Spadaro, G., & Balliet, D. (2020). Personality and prosocial behavior: A theoretical framework and meta-analysis. Psychological Bulletin, 146(1), 30. I also found: Ding, F., & Lu, Z. (2016). Association between empathy and prosocial behavior: A systematic review and meta-analysis. Advances in Psychological Science, 24(8), 1159. Yin, Y., & Wang, Y. (2023). Is empathy associated with more prosocial behaviour? A meta‐analysis. Asian Journal of Social Psychology, 26(1), 3-22.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2: The article's reports striking, original findings that make a crucial empirical contribution to the perennial debate about the nature of human altruism. The findings from experiments on charitable giving suggest that emotion drives charitable giving, whereas rational considerations about the donation's effectiveness are practically irrelevant to lay people's decisions of which charity to donate to. At the same time, the authors' meta-analysis of findings from correlational studies suggests that people might be deceiving themselves and/or others into thinking that the charities they donate to are more effective than those they didn't donate to. The article's findings significantly advance research on the psychology of (in)effective altruism, charitable giving, and several related fields. This is the first meta-analysis of research on the role of effectiveness considerations in charitable giving. To my knowledge, this is the first, authoritative direct comparison of the actual, causal effect of effectiveness considerations to people's post-hoc rationalizations of their decisions. This comparison revealed a crucial discrepancy between what people say and what people do. The methodology is sound, and the conclusions are well-supported by rigorous meta-analyses of the largest data set that has ever been brought to bear on these questions. The Methods section could benefit from additional information about how the effect sizes were computed for studies with experimental designs and how they were converted into r values. Relatedly, in Lines 197-200 of the Results section, the description of the difference between studies in which effectiveness was measured and studies in which it was manipulated should be more clear and more detailed. There is no reason why experiments that manipulate effectiveness couldn't also measure people's perceptions of effectiveness. It thus remains unclear whether the effects reported for experiments are associations between donations and experimentally induced perceptions of effectiveness or, as I assume, associations between the experimental manipulation and donations. This should be clarified. There also appears to be a rendering error in Lines 204-205 ("r=.??, p=.??"). I think adding information about how the effect sizes were computed for different study designs will be crucial to make the findings reproducible. In the interest of reproducibility, I think the authors should also release the data extracted from the articles, the scripts used to compute effect sizes from that information, and the computed effect sizes. I think the authors should also report confidence intervals on the reported effect size estimates. Explicit statistical comparisons between the effects of effectiveness and empathy would also be informative.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3: Hi, I don’t have to much to say about this paper. My one main concern is it isn’t so obvious how to interpret this exercise. That is, it seems quite conceivable to me that efficiency perceptions/manipulations could be strongly/weakly correlated with giving behavior in laboratory experiments, even if they do/don’t correlate with real world giving behavior. Likewise, it is not clear to me that could compare the effects in the efficiency literature to the effects in the empathy literature to conclude that empathy is more or less significant for real world giving. It could just be, for instance, that the variation/manipulations in one of these literatures are particularly weak or strong, compared to the variation/manipulations real world charities use. Perhaps also efficiency matters more in some contexts rather than others, e.g. when side by side comparisons are possible or norms specify concern for efficiency? In which case, again, it is not clear how much we can learn from the r squared in experiments where the contexts may quite different from the real world. Perhaps the authors can speak to these issues a bit more?
reviewer_comments.reviewer_4: This paper reports the results of a meta-analysis exploring the relationships between perceived effectiveness and empathy with charitable giving. This is certainly a worthwhile and interesting project, and I appreciate the effort that goes into a meta-analysis. My evaluation of the research itself (the methods and reporting of the results) is mostly positive. But I do have somewhat large concerns regarding the framing of the research question and interpretation of the results. 1. The authors confuse “effectiveness” with “perceived effectiveness” throughout the manuscript. The meta-analysis only looks at perceived effectiveness and not actual effectiveness. Consequently, the results do not shed light on whether people are “effective altruists”. Presumably, many effective altruists would agree that perceived effectiveness differs starkly from actual effectiveness (and possibly that empathy itself may be correlated with (mis)perceived effectiveness). This is precisely why they think their cold calculations are needed to estimate effectiveness--because human intuition cannot be trusted. I thus think the introductory material and the conclusions/discussion surrounding effective altruism are mostly irrelevant to the current project. More generally, I think the introduction and general discussion should be rewritten to be more appropriate for the present meta-analysis, which I explain more below. 2. The authors overinterpret the importance of the difference between correlational and experimental results. A lack of experimental evidence does not mean there is no causal relationship. Experimental tests are one way to estimate causal relationships, but a failure to find them does not disprove them. The discussion of a “paradox” is thus unwarranted based on the current data. Any one manipulation might fail for countless reasons (e.g., people already have entrenched beliefs that cannot be changed with a 5 minute manipulation). The correlational results suggest that perceived effectiveness may be an important predictor of charitable giving. The conclusions should call for more research on the potential causal relationship rather than asserting it has been ruled out. 3. Relatedly, claims comparing the relative evidence for “empathy” vs. “effectiveness” seem unwarranted. First, the authors do not statistically test for differences between the effectiveness and empathy explanations. Second, it is inappropriate to disregard the correlation between perceived effectiveness and charitable giving in this comparison. Third, perceived effectiveness and empathy might be positively related. If the data are available, it would be helpful to report (1) the meta-analyzed associations between perceived effectiveness and empathy, and (2) the meta-analyzed manipulation checks for the empathy and effectiveness manipulations (so we know whether those manipulations were successful, how large the manipulation effects were, and whether they were equally successful). 4. The authors acknowledge that they cannot comment on arguments for or against “effective altruism” or for or against “against empathy”, yet these are the primary focuses of the abstract, introduction, and much of the discussion. I agree that the present project does not speak much to these movements/arguments. These data do not tell us whether people are (or should be) effective altruists, only that perceived effectiveness is related to charitable giving. And these data do not tell us whether people have too much or too little empathy, only that empathy appears to be a contributing factor to charitable giving. I thus think the framing of the paper as a potential challenge to those perspectives is inappropriate. A more neutral and accurate framing of the paper would be a simple focus on its own contribution—testing the extents to which empathy and perceived effectiveness relate to charitable giving. 5. Relatedly, in my view, the tone of the paper seems inappropriate for a science paper. The paper seems to lament that other scholars have received attention for their work in this space. The paper would have a more scientific tone if the introduction simply explained what was known to date and set up the open questions. Additionally, the paper should avoid exaggerating the conclusiveness of the results (e.g., “provide an authoritative answer…”). Scientific conclusions are generally tentative, not definitive. 6. The authors submitted their paper with some internal comments still visible. This raised concerns regarding transparency and awareness of their own data. For example, one internal comment stated “We originally had 31 but dropped the 2 “local” effects. We also had two missing effect sizes last time, but I’m presuming that these were included in the 31 count even though the effect sizes weren’t included in the calculations?” What does this mean? Why were effects dropped? What are the results with and without them? And why would two missing effect sizes be included in the reported number of effect sizes? 7. Additionally, this sentence was included with missing information: “After removing this effect size, a significant (but still modest) positive relationship emerged (r = .??, p = .??).” The r and p values should be added. 8. I was puzzled by this statement: “It should be noted that 1 of the 29 effect sizes was based on a very large sample (>11,000) and so had an out-sized influence on the overall mean effect.” The authors claim to have used a random effects model, in which case the effect sizes would not be weighted by sample size. Is there an explanation for this? 9. If the authors would like to comment on the potential effectiveness of effective-altruism-like interventions, they should separately report the results of the 22 studies that taught participants about effective altruism (and also resolve the internal disagreement among co-authors [seen in their tracked comments] about which studies fit this criterion). 10. The internal comments regarding this sentence are also concerning: “On the upside, over 80% of the effect sizes were drawn from non-student samples, and 32% measured actual donation behaviour as opposed to an intention or some other proxy of behaviour.” One co-author commented on how these calculations might be wrong, and the other commented that they were never done in the first place. 11. The abstract should report the number of included papers and studies in addition to effect sizes and total n. Despite these many issues, I do think the meta-analysis itself could be of interest to many people, including scholars interested in the effective altruism movement. I hope my comments will help the authors avoid likely criticisms of the current version of the manuscript.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_5: Thank you for the opportunity to review this manuscript. While the topic is important, the manuscript needs greater detail in the methods section. Below are methodological issues that need to be clarified. The abstract and manuscript itself imply that the meta-analysis results can answer a causal question, namely whether perceptions of effectiveness and empathy cause greater charitable giving. The word “shaped” implies causal inference, however meta-analyses are secondary studies and cannot make causal inferences. In addition, the synthesis includes a mix of studies, some correlational/observational and others reporting on experiments. The inclusion of both types of studies limits the review’s ability to discuss whether primary studies have established a causal relationship between perceptions of effectiveness and empathy. The abstract provides the average correlation between given and both effectiveness and empathy but does not provide the standard error of this estimate or the amount of heterogeneity present. The average correlation is important information, but it is equally important to understand how much variation exists across studies. The abstract needs to include both the standard error for the mean effect size to assess whether the correlation is significantly different from zero, and a measure of the heterogeneity across studies. See below for more discussion of the reporting of heterogeneity in this review. There is a mismatch between the aims of the paper and the types of studies included. Page 4, line 65 of the manuscript states that “the goal of this paper is to add an important missing piece to the debate: meta-analyses of the extent to which people are, in fact, influenced by effectiveness and empathy in making charitable decisions.” It appears that both correlational and experimental studies were included in this review. Only experimental studies that manipulate effectiveness and empathy can provide a direct estimate of the causal relationship between effectiveness and empathy and giving. The correlational studies can only examine the association between giving and perceived effectiveness and empathy. These two types of studies are addressing different research questions. It is unclear the nature of the studies included in this review, and how they address the key aim of the review. The search and screening methods need more detail. Searching. The manuscript reports examples of search terms but best practice is to include the exact search strings used for each database and the dates each search was carried out on each database. This information is often reported in the appendix. The review should include an Inclusion Criteria section describing in detail the population studied, all included study designs and outcomes. A rationale for the types of study designs should also be provided; the nature of the study designs included is unclear as described above. All of the included definitions of donation effectiveness and empathy should be described in this section. Additionally, definitions of constructs such as giving intention, amount of charitable giving., manipulated given and measured giving should be provided. The English language and publication date specifications will also be included in the Inclusion Criteria section as will any limitations on countries of origin. Screening. It is unclear in the manuscript how many screeners were used for each stage of the screening process. A double-screening process is standard practice to guard against any bias in this stage. This section should also report the process by which the authors determined the eligibility of each study and the order in which each item was addressed for both the title and abstract screening and full-text review. If a screening guide was used, include it in the appendix. This section should also describe the screeners and the training or preparation (i.e. pilot screening, etc.) they received. The 2015 Haddaway guidelines have been updated with more recent evidence. Google Scholar is no longer a recommended search system for evidence synthesis, because the searches are not reproducible. For more information, see the citation below. Gusenbauer, M. and Haddaway, N.R. (2019). Which academic search systems are suitable for systematic reviews or meta-analysis? Evaluating retrieval qualities of Google Scholar, PubMed, and 26 other resources. Research Synthesis Methods. DOI: 10.1002/jrsm.1378 Unpublished literature included in the review is limited to Google Scholar searches. The authors might consider refreshing their unpublished research search by searching dissertation and thesis databases or websites of related organizations. The coding process and included items is unclear. A coding section describes the process used to extract data from studies. Each item coded should be described either in narrative form or by providing the codebook. The coding section reports the number of coders, their experience levels, and any training they received including pilot coding. It is also unclear if the review included any critical appraisal/rating of study quality of the included studies. It is unclear how effect sizes were coded in the review. It is unclear how effect sizes were coded in this review. The review reports correlations, but experimental studies may provide information that would typically be synthesized in the form of a standardized mean difference or a mean difference if studies used the same outcome measure. It is unclear if standardized mean differences were converted to correlations, and what conversion formula was used. In addition, it is unclear how effect sizes were computed from correlation studies. It is unclear if the review limited the effect sizes to reported bivariate correlations or if bivariate correlations were estimated from other statistics such as regression coefficients. The section on publication bias indicates that only published studies were used in exploring potential selection bias. It is unclear why only published articles were used in the analyses exploring the potential impact of selection bias in this review. Publication bias concerns whether the overall estimates have the potential of bias due to small sample effects; deleting the unpublished studies provides an incomplete view of the evidence base. The review should use Egger’s sandwich test given the presence of dependent effect sizes. The manuscript reports three different tests for publication bias, but these tests are inappropriate when there are multiple effect sizes nested within studies. Egger’s sandwich tests funnel plot symmetry with dependent effect sizes. Please see the following reference for more information. Rodgers, M. A., & Pustejovsky, J. E. (2021). Evaluating meta-analytic methods to detect selective reporting in the presence of dependent effect sizes. Psychological Methods, 26(2), 141–160. https://doi.org/10.1037/met0000300 The manuscript should discuss heterogeneity in more detail. Page 8 of the manuscript describes the relative amount of variation at each level but does not provide the overall estimate of heterogeneity. The manuscript should report the within-study and between-study variance components for the model and use these components to report the prediction interval for the two main correlations. It is unclear how much studies vary in their estimates of the two key correlations. See below for a reference about reporting the prediction interval: Borenstein, M., Higgins, J. P. T., Hedges, L. V., & Rothstein, H. R. (2017). Basics of meta-analysis: I2 is not an absolute measure of heterogeneity. Research Synthesis Methods, 8(1), 5–18. https://doi.org/10.1002/jrsm.1230 Consider using meta-regression to analyze moderators. Table 1 appears to report single-variable moderator analysis. The limitation of this approach is that it is unclear how the moderators used in Table 1 relate to one another. With 259 effect sizes, the analysis can use multiple meta-regression with multiple moderators in a single model. Meta-regression can also accommodate both continuous and categorical in a single model. See the reference below for best practice in meta-regression: Tipton, E., Pustejovsky, J. E., & Ahmadi, H. (2019). A history of meta-regression: Technical, conceptual, and practical developments between 1974 and 2018. Research Synthesis Methods, 2(10), 161–179. https://doi.org/10.1002/jrsm.1338 Editing comments. The manuscript contained authors’ comments to each other On page 9, line 205, there is “??” where a number was intended. Terri Pigott, PhD, Georgia State University with the assistance of Natalie Pruitt, MS, Georgia State University

peer_review_rounds.author_response: RESPONSE TO REVIEWERS We thank the five reviewers for your patience in receiving this revision; critical re-analyses had to wait for the 2nd author to return from maternity leave. In response to your very helpful suggestions, we have made several revisions. Most notably, we have remodelled the Introduction, included more details about our searching and screening processes, conducted several new analyses, and expanded the discussion. Below, we describe in detail how we have responded to each of your comments. In light of these changes, we believe the paper now makes a clearer, stronger and more focused contribution. We thank you for the time you have put into facilitating these improvements. Best regards, The authors REVIEWER 1 In a meta analyses of 416 effect sizes from 74,797 participants, the authors examine the extent by which charitable giving is shaped by perceptions of effectiveness versus empathy. They find that self-reported effectiveness perceptions explain more variance in charitable giving than empathy, but effectiveness interventions do not reliably influence charitable giving. This is my first time reviewing this paper. I appreciated the opportunity to read this work. The key strength of the paper is the inclusion of two large-scale meta-analyses aggregating an impressive number of studies on charitable giving, which provide a nuanced perspective about the extent to which empathy and effectiveness perceptions motivate charitable giving and confirm rather paradoxical behaviors that people self-report in ways that imply effectiveness is very important to them, but seem relatively unmoved by actual effectiveness information. With reasonable updates, I think this work will be of interest to a broad readership. These are the things I suggest to help make the paper stronger: We thank Reviewer 1 for their thoughtful and constructive advice. The introduction—notably the 2nd, 3rd, and 4th paragraphs—set up a debate about “empathic” versus “effective” altruism, but then state that the “goal of this paper is not to weigh up the moral arguments of the effective altruism movement or the case against empathy” but to conduct “meta-analyses of the extent to which people are, in fact, influenced by effectiveness and empathy in making charitable decisions” (pg 3). This was quite striking to me for several reasons. First, Bloom’s arguments are not that people do not engage in empathic charitable giving, but that it may be unfair or less effective at actually helping. Second, and more importantly, much work over the last decade suggests 2 that empathic and effective altruism are more compatible than previously argued (e.g., Everett et al., 2018; Fowler et al., 2021; Law et al., 2022, 2024). Setting up this debate in order to ask “to what extent does empathy or effectiveness drive charitable giving?” seems misleading and distracting from the main study. An alternative motivation might be best described by the authors in the Discussion, which focus on the following questions: Is charitable giving overly influenced by empathy? Is charitable giving under-influenced by analytical, cost-benefit analyses about maximising good? How successful is empathy induction in promoting charitable giving? How successful are effectiveness interventions in promoting charitable giving? Readers may benefit more by motivating your study from this perspective and providing additional background on evidence for the "effectiveness paradox" rather than the empathy versus effectiveness debate. Everett, J. A., Faber, N. S., Savulescu, J., & Crockett, M. J. (2018). The costs of being consequentialist: Social inference from instrumental harm and impartial beneficence. Journal of Experimental Social Psychology, 79, 200-216. Fowler, Z., Law, K. F., & Gaesser, B. (2021). Against empathy bias: The moral value of equitable empathy. Psychological Science, 32(5), 766-779. Law, K. F., Amormino, P., Marsh, A. A., & O’Connor, B. B. (2024). Ethical reasoning versus empathic bias: A false dichotomy? Trends in Cognitive Sciences, 28(1), 1–4. Law, K. F., Campbell, D., & Gaesser, B. (2022). Biased benevolence: The perceived morality of effective altruism across social distance. Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin, 48(3), 426-444. We thank Reviewer 1 for pushing us on this point. In light of these comments, as well as related comments from other reviewers, we have remodelled the Introduction. The 2nd, 3rd and 4th paragraphs highlighted above have been collapsed into one paragraph, deleting much of the previous discussion of the philosophical origins and cultural currency of the effective altruism movement. This provides a more focused introduction to our key questions. We also appreciate the opportunity to incorporate Reviewer 1’s suggested references into the paper. Together, these studies argue that empathy is not inherently narrow or biased (Fowler et al., 2021); people value impartial altruism when not paired with harm (Everett et al., 2018); effective altruism can be viewed as competent and moral, even when directed toward strangers (Law et al., 2022); and the notion that empathy and effectiveness are psychologically opposed is a false dichotomy (Law et al., 2024). We have added a sentence to the re-modelled Introduction to reflect this more integrative perspective: “Although some of these earlier critiques positioned empathy and effectiveness as competing motives, recent evidence suggests they may be mutually reinforcing—particularly when empathic concern is broadened to include distant others and is guided by reasoning about impact (Everett et al., 2018; Fowler et al., 2021; Law et al., 2022, 2024).” It appears that the authors run separate models for empathy and effectiveness and then qualitatively compare the effect sizes from each of the models to draw their conclusions (e.g., that perceived effectiveness predicts charitable giving over and above empathy). Is there a way to statistically compare these effect sizes directly? The authors might be limited by having no or few studies that measure both empathy and effectiveness (were there any that measured both?), but comparing effect sizes would immensely improve the inferences drawn by the results. If not, then this should be noted as a limitation. 3 This comment applied to the following passage in the Discussion of the original manuscript: “Correlationally, effectiveness ratings are considerably bigger predictors of charitable giving than empathy, explaining more than three times the variance (17% versus 5%). If one were to focus just on the correlational evidence, then, one might reach the conclusion that Bloom’s thesis in Against Empathy was alarmist: people’s charitable giving is in fact associated with judgements about effectiveness, and much more so than it is with empathy.” We agree with Reviewer 1: statements that the meta-analytic effect for effectiveness is bigger than that for empathy are inappropriate in the absence of formal significance tests. As Reviewer 1 anticipated, however, we are restricted here by the fact that only 9 studies measured both empathy and effectiveness, making a formal meta-regression test under-powered. A z-test for comparing two independent effect sizes confirmed that the correlational effect of effectiveness was indeed bigger than the correlational effect for empathy (z = -2.01, p = .044) but this test assumes that the two sets of studies are non-overlapping. We re-calculated the z-test removing the overlapping studies, and the result was exactly the same, but the deletion of effect sizes from the corpus is not ideal. After much discussion within the team, we could find no elegant way of walking the reader through all this. Given this statistical quandary, we decided to simply rephrase the above passage so as not to imply that we are formally comparing the size of the two effects (which is also more in keeping with the revised frame described above). We would like to keep the description of variance explained though, which we think is sufficient to tell the story of the data. Revised text: “When people self-report the effectiveness of a charity or charitable act, it has a medium-to-large association with giving (r = .42). In other words, perceptions of effectiveness explain approximately 17% of variance in charitable giving (to benchmark this, empathy explained only 5%).” The authors focus on charitable giving, a well-studied and valid form of altruistic giving. How do they speculate their findings generalizing to other forms of altruism, such as stem cell donation or organ donation? Interestingly, the results show that self-reports of empathy are robustly associated with charitable giving. How do the authors reconcile these findings which recent work finding that self-reports of empathic concern are not robust predictors of other forms of real-world altruism (Rhoads et al., 2023)? Do the authors believe there is something specific about the relationship between empathic motivation and acts of charitable giving—perhaps the relative cost of charitable donations is lower or perhaps acts of charity are more outward forms of social or moral signaling linked to social desirability biases or norms? Rhoads, S. A., Vekaria, K. M., O’Connell, K., Elizabeth, H. S., Rand, D. G., Kozak Williams, M. N., & Marsh, A. A. (2023). Unselfish traits and social decision-making patterns characterize six populations of real-world extraordinary altruists. Nature Communications, 14(1), 1807. We thank the reviewer for this thoughtful question. In response we have added the following paragraph to the Discussion: “Although charitable giving is a valid and well-studied expression of altruism, it is only one form among many. It remains an open question whether the patterns we observe here generalise to other forms of altruism that carry higher personal costs, such as organ donation, 4 stem cell registration, or direct physical aid. For instance, Rhoads and colleagues found that self-reported empathic concern was not a consistent predictor of real-world extraordinary altruism in these domains across six populations of altruistic individuals. Charitable giving may be more strongly influenced by empathy because it is (a) low-cost, (b) normatively endorsed, and (c) easily enacted. Additionally, some other forms of prosocial behaviour (e.g., volunteering, organ donation, sperm donation) provide more direct payoffs to the “giver” and so may be less empathically motivated. We encourage future research to test whether the role of empathy in charitable giving is driven by these contextual features, and to explore whether different psychological profiles underlie high-cost versus low-cost altruism.” The authors need a table either in main text or supporting information describing the specific measures used in each of the studies included their analyses and how they were classified. I did not see any description of this and thus it was difficult for me to interpret any of the results. For example, what does “Behavioural” mean in Table 2? Which behavioural measures of giving were used? This practice is fairly standard in meta-analysis papers. In the revision we point readers to the excel spreadsheet of the dataset on OSF. This spreadsheet contains written notes on specific measures used and how they were subsequently classified into the levels of the moderators. We have also added some brief written clarification in the manuscript itself at the first mention of the behavioural vs self-report distinction: “First, the association was significantly stronger when charitable giving was self-reported (e.g., willingness to donate, future intentions to donate, self-reported past giving; r = .38, p < .001) than when studies used behavioural measures of giving (e.g., direct observations of giving in the field, the amount of a study payment that the participant donated; r = .27, p < .001).” Perceived Effectiveness: I suggest the author stick with the term “perceived effectiveness” when discussing self-report effectiveness but describe it earlier. Throughout the manuscript, we refer to “perceived effectiveness” when referring to the correlational effects. Typo on Line 205: “r = .??, p = .??” Apologies for the embarrassing oversight. This and other minor glitches are due to the fact that we submitted the next-to-last version of the manuscript rather than the final version. A reminder of the context here: 1 of the 29 effect sizes was based on a very large sample (>11,000) and so the first author wanted to check whether it had an out-sized influence on the overall mean effect. When we saw that the meta-analytic effect size barely changed, it was pointed out by the second author that we used a random effects model and so the effect sizes were not weighted by sample size (a point made also by Reviewer 4). For this reason, this passage was deleted in the “final” draft (that was accidentally not submitted) and is deleted also from our revised version. Lines 91-93: The authors state “the last meta-analysis on the link between empathy and prosocial behaviour was published over 35 years ago, and incorporated only a handful of studies on charitable giving.” However, meta-analytic studies have investigated the relationship between empathy and prosociality since Eisenberg & Miller (1987), notably: Thielmann, I., Spadaro, G., & Balliet, D. (2020). Personality and prosocial behavior: A 5 theoretical framework and meta-analysis. Psychological Bulletin, 146(1), 30. I also found: Ding, F., & Lu, Z. (2016). Association between empathy and prosocial behavior: A systematic review and meta-analysis. Advances in Psychological Science, 24(8), 1159. Yin, Y., & Wang, Y. (2023). Is empathy associated with more prosocial behaviour? A meta‐analysis. Asian Journal of Social Psychology, 26(1), 3-22. We thank Reviewer 1 for directing us to this research, which we now acknowledge in the revised manuscript: “Empirical synthesis is overdue: the first meta-analysis on the link between empathy and prosocial behaviour was published nearly 40 years ago and incorporated only a handful of studies on charitable giving (Eisenberg & Miller, 1987). Subsequent syntheses have not examined experimental work, focusing exclusively on correlational links between measures of empathy and questionnaire measures of dispositional pro-social behaviour (Ding & Lu, 2016; Yin & Wang, 2023) or between measures of empathy and resource allocations in lab-based games such as the Dictator Game and the Prisoner’s Dilemma (Thielmann et al., 2020).” To elaborate on the three new references that have been included: The meta-analyses reported by Ding and Lu (2016) and Yin and Wang (2023) focus only on correlational research. Specifically, they examined only papers that measured empathy (dispositionally) and also measured pro-social behaviour as a dispositional trait (using scales such as Prosocial Behaviour Questionnaire, Prosocial Motivation Scale, Prosocialness Scale for Adults, Prosocial Tendencies Measure, Prosocial Tendencies Measure, and so forth). In both cases the meta-analyses only included papers that reported bivariate correlations. Where regressions were reported, the authors of these meta-analyses did not contact the authors of the original studies to obtain correlations; the study was simply left out of the meta-analysis. The Thielmann et al. (2020) meta-analysis was much more rigorous but focused only on personality dimensions (of which one was empathy, construed as a sub-facet of HEXACO) and their correlation with decisions made in 6 games: Dictator Game, Ultimatum Game, Trust Game, Prisoner’s Dilemma, Public Goods Game, Commons Dilemma. Given this – and mindful of the fact that there has been no meta-analysis on effectiveness at all – we think the claim “empirical synthesis is overdue” is warranted. REVIEWER 2 The article's reports striking, original findings that make a crucial empirical contribution to the perennial debate about the nature of human altruism. The findings from experiments on charitable giving suggest that emotion drives charitable giving, whereas rational considerations about the donation's effectiveness are practically irrelevant to lay people's decisions of which charity to donate to. At the same time, the authors' meta-analysis of findings from correlational studies suggests that people might be deceiving themselves and/or others into thinking that the charities they donate to are more effective than those they didn't donate to. The article's findings significantly advance research on the psychology of (in)effective altruism, charitable giving, and several related fields. This is the first meta-analysis of research on the role of effectiveness considerations in charitable giving. To my knowledge, this is the first, authoritative direct comparison of the actual, causal effect of effectiveness considerations to people's post-hoc rationalizations of their decisions. As such, we worry that highlighting this information early in the Method section would potentially lead to confusion (i.e., telling the statistical story backwards). Reviewer #5: The revised version of the manuscript addresses many of the concerns we raised in the first review. However, there remain issues that need to be clarified. 1. Please add the fact that there is significant heterogeneity among studies in their estimates of the correlations in the abstract. The abstract provides the mean correlation and its confidence interval, but does not indicate that there is significant heterogeneity in this estimate as demonstrated in the prediction intervals. Please see Tipton et al. (2023) for a demonstration of the importance of discussing effect size heterogeneity. Tipton, E., Bryan, C., Murray, J., McDaniel, M. A., Schneider, B., & Yeager, D. S. (2023). Why meta-analyses of growth mindset and other interventions should follow best practices for examining heterogeneity: Commentary on Macnamara and Burgoyne (2023) and Burnette et al. (2023).
