While the univariate analyses are interesting, they are subject to potential confounding. This is clear in the meta-regression analysis including all moderators. The self-reported and behavioral measures difference is no longer significant when including all moderators. Thus, the meta-regression results should be the analysis that is interpreted more extensively than the individual univariate analyses. The current manuscript highlights the univariate analyses, and provides a narrative description only of the meta-regression. Since meta-regression and meta-analyses suffer from potential overlapping and confounding moderators, the meta-regression results allow the interpretation of the association among the moderators and the correlations controlling for other moderators. The meta-regression can be estimated in a way to obtain the adjusted subgroup means by deleting the intercept term and thus, the discussion about subgroup differences could use the adjusted means rather than the means from univariate meta-regressions. Table 4 should be the main analysis here. Please see Tipton et al. (2019) for a discussion of meta-regression. Tipton, E., Pustejovsky, J. E., & Ahmadi, H. (2019). Current practices in meta-regression in psychology, education, and medicine. Research Synthesis Methods, 10(2), 180–194. https://doi.org/10.1002/jrsm.1339 Thank you for your thoughtful comments regarding the interpretation of our univariate and multivariate meta-regression analyses. We agree that multivariate meta-regression provides important insights by accounting for potential confounding among moderators. To help clarify why some moderator effects observed in the univariate models did not persist in the multivariate model, we have added a paragraph to the Results section explaining that the no-longer-significant effects (i.e., the moderating roles of self-report vs. behavioural measures, and likelihood vs. value) were likely suppressed due to their shared variance with the measured vs. manipulated distinction. Experimental studies were more likely to use behavioural and value-based outcomes, making it difficult with the current data to completely disentangle their independent effects. Nevertheless, we would like to clarify and justify our analytic strategy, which follows a staged approach to moderator analysis. Specifically, we first conduct univariate meta-regressions to identify potentially influential moderators and then estimate a multivariate model using only those that showed meaningful effects. This approach is well-established in the meta-analytic literature (e.g., Borenstein et al., 2009; Lipsey & Wilson, 2001) and was particularly appropriate given the structure of our data. For example, not all studies included information on every moderator, and our goal was to retain as many studies as possible in each analysis. Conducting a full multivariate model from the outset would have required listwise deletion, significantly reducing the sample size and, in turn, statistical power. Power would also be further reduced by including too many predictors in the model simultaneously. By using univariate models, we were able to include the full set of studies available for each moderator, reducing the potential for bias that can arise when missing data are not random, and thereby provide a more accurate and inclusive picture of the evidence. Indeed, while Tipton et al. (2019) advocate for careful interpretation of meta-regression results, they also recognise that staged approaches - beginning with univariate moderator analyses as we have done - are a common strategy, particularly when moderator data are not fully reported across studies or when model complexity may exceed available power. 5 We thank the reviewer also for raising the possibility of presenting adjusted subgroup means from the multivariate meta-regression model by removing the intercept term. We agree this is a useful strategy in some contexts and appreciate the methodological clarity it can offer. Given the number of moderators in our models and the limited number of effect sizes available for some cells, estimating adjusted means for every subgroup in this way would have introduced instability and reduced interpretability in our already complex models. Instead, we chose to report the coefficient-based contrasts (relative to reference categories) from the multivariate model, and present univariate subgroup means to aid interpretation of the raw patterns in the data. We believe this approach offers a reasonable balance of rigour and accessibility, but we are happy to revisit this decision if the editor or reviewers feel strongly. Borenstein, M., Hedges, L. V., Higgins, J. P. T., & Rothstein, H. R. (2009). Introduction to meta-analysis. Wiley. Lipsey, M. W., & Wilson, D. B. (2001). Practical meta-analysis. Sage Publications. 3. On page 11, line 265, this statement appears, referring to the average correlation in the meta-analysis: “This association was robust, emerging across diverse samples and operationalisations of charitable giving.” This statement is misleading as there is significant heterogeneity across the studies, with a prediction interval ranging from -0.14 to 0.57. The lack of statistical significance for the association among moderators and the correlation does not negate the fact that the studies are reporting a wide range of associations from negative to positive. We have revised the sentence in question to better capture the robustness of the overall effect while clearly signalling the variability in effect sizes across studies. It now reads: “This association was statistically robust across a wide range of samples and operationalisations of charitable giving, although significant heterogeneity was observed.” 4. On page 20, line 472, the manuscript describes the multilevel model used for the analysis. The authors might consider highlighting the assumption in the multilevel model that the effect sizes within studies are considered independent. The multilevel model is one potential model used for dependent effect sizes; Pustejovsky & Tipton (202 ) discuss other models such as the correlated and hierarchical model (the multilevel model assuming a nonzero correlation among effect sizes nested within studies). Pustejovsky, J. E., & Tipton, E. (2021). Meta-analysis with Robust Variance Estimation: Expanding the Range of Working Models. Prevention Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11121-021-01246-3 Thank you for raising this important point regarding the assumptions underlying our multilevel model. To clarify, the three-level meta-analytic model we used (following Assink & Wibbelink, 2016) does not assume independence of effect sizes within studies. Rather, it explicitly models the dependence through a nested random effects structure, with separate variance components at the within-study (Level 2) and between-study (Level 3) levels. In this sense, our model accounts for non-independence among effect sizes by allowing for heterogeneity at both the study and effect levels. We recognise, however, that this approach assumes no residual correlation among effect sizes within studies beyond what is captured by the random effects. As noted in Pustejovsky and 6 Tipton (2021), more flexible models - such as those that specify a residual correlation structure or use robust variance estimation - offer alternatives that can accommodate more complex dependence patterns, especially when many effect sizes are drawn from each study. We have revised the Methods section to make this modelling assumption more explicit and have added reference to Pustejovsky & Tipton (2021) to acknowledge these alternative approaches. Given the relatively small number of effect sizes per study in our dataset (average of 2.24), we judged the three-level model to be appropriate and parsimonious for our purposes. We nevertheless appreciate the importance of adding this additional clarity in our Methods. Therefore, we have added the following in the Method: “Specifically, the total variance is partitioned into three components: sampling variance (Level 1), within-study variance (Level 2), and between-study variance (Level 3), thereby accounting for the non-independence of effect sizes within studies. We note, however, that the model assumes residuals are uncorrelated within studies beyond the modelled random effects (Pustejovsky & Tipton, 2021).” 5. The manuscript still includes a few causal statements. On pages 3 and 11 (“to what extent”), and page 8 (“impacted”). On page 8, we changed the sentence “Finally, we examined whether the different operationalisations of effectiveness impacted strength of association” to “Finally, we examined whether the different operationalisations of effectiveness corresponded to differences in strength of association”. We appreciate the concern about potential causal inference. We chose the phrasing "to what extent" to indicate degree or magnitude of association, not directionality or causality. This phrase is commonly used in both correlational and experimental contexts, and we believe it accurately reflects the descriptive and quantitative nature of our synthesis. .6. Page 8, line 176 includes a typo, “was perceived to be had no reliable effect”. The original sentence was “In other words, experimental stimuli designed to manipulate how effective a donation or charity was perceived to be had no reliable effect on charitable giving choices”. Although this is not a typo, we agree that the sentence was convoluted and vulnerable to misreading. We have now changed it to “In other words, experimental stimuli intended to influence perceptions of a charity’s effectiveness did not reliably affect charitable giving decisions on average.” 1 RESPONSE TO REVIEWER COMMENTS Reviewer #1: I thank the authors for their revisions. My concerns have been satisfactorily addressed. We thank Reviewer 1 for their contributions to the paper. Reviewer #5: Thank you for this careful revision. My prior comments are now addressed. I have one additional clarification regarding the results of the univariate moderator analyses. In Table 2, each section of the table reports on a single subgroup analysis, comparing the mean effect size from, for example, studies measuring state versus trait empathy. The text on page 10 notes that "a stronger association was found when empathy was operationalised situationally (i.e., as a state variable; r=.27, p<.001) than when it was measured dispositionally (i.e., as a trait variable; r=.20, p<.001)". How was this test conducted to make the claim that the correlation of r=0.27 is stronger than r=0.20? Was there a statistical test conducted to examine these differences in an ANOVA-like framework or using a Wald test with contrasts in meta-regression? Many of the univariate subgroup means have overlapping 95% confidence intervals so it is difficult to see how conclusions were drawn from these analyses. For all categorical moderators (including the state vs trait empathy example), we did not infer subgroup differences from visual inspection of the confidence intervals. In these models, the moderator was included as a dummy-coded predictor, and the F-statistic reported in Tables 1 and 2 is a Wald-type omnibus test of the moderator (i.e., an ANOVA-like test of whether the average effect differs across categories). In the specific example the reviewer highlights, the difference between state empathy (r = .27) and trait empathy (r = .20) comes from such a model, and the omnibus test was significant, F(1,254) = 7.06, p = .008. Our statement that the association is “stronger” for state than trait empathy is therefore based on this omnibus test of the difference between subgroup effects, not on overlapping 95% CIs around the subgroup means. As the reviewer notes, overlapping CIs for the two subgroup means can occur even when the CI for their difference excludes zero, which is what the omnibus test captures.

review_generation.input:
You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications, one of the world's leading multidisciplinary journals.

Read the following paper carefully and write a thorough, technically rigorous peer review. Identify the most important scientific concerns regarding: methodology, statistical analysis, data quality, claims vs. evidence, reproducibility, and clarity. Organise your review with clear sections.

## Abstract

Effective altruists argue that charitable giving is over-influenced by empathic responses and should
instead be guided by cost-benefit analyses about the effectiveness of giving. To provide insight into the
extent to which empathy and effectiveness are associated with charitable giving in the population, two
meta-analyses are conducted, synthesising 416 effect sizes from 124 papers sampling 74,797
participants. Here we show that effectiveness, r = .34, SE = .04, 95%CIs [.28, .40], and empathy, r =
.25, SE = .02, CIs [.21, .29], both positively relate to charitable giving overall. However, prediction
intervals reveal significant heterogeneity. Moderation analyses reveal one crucial caveat to the overall
association between effectiveness and charitable giving: although the mean effect is relatively large
when effectiveness is measured, r = .42, CIs [.35, .48], manipulated effectiveness has a weak effect, r =
.03, CIs [-.10, .17]. Our findings suggest that while people may self-perceive as effective altruists, they
give like empathic ones, a disjunction that calls for deeper causal investigation.

---

## Introduction

Understanding why and to what extent people engage in charitable giving has long been a
preoccupation of social scientists.1 One reason for this is that charitable giving serves an important
function in sustaining a healthy and inclusive society. Estimated at over $470 billion per year in the U.S.
alone2, charitable giving funds help, care, and services in ways that cannot be readily substituted
through commercial or government activities. As such, charitable giving is designed to enrich lives, and
in many cases to save lives. Another reason charitable giving has preoccupied scholars is its symbolic
value in signifying the degree to which people engage in kindness and compassion to others.
Understanding charitable giving helps us understand who we are as humans, and how we express our
humanity.

One of the biggest debates about charitable giving – both within and outside academia – is
whether people rely too much on their “heart” when giving, and not enough on their “head”. In his book
Against Empathy3 – and in high-profile opinion pieces4 – Paul Bloom makes the case that empathy is a
poor moral guide to charitable giving. In line with the empathy-altruism hypothesis5,6, Bloom agrees
that empathy plays a role in activating the motivation to do good. However, it also leads us to make
ineffective or unfair charitable decisions, focusing on issues that respond to our immediate emotional
triggers rather than grounding our compassion in rational deliberation about which causes do most good
(i.e., effectiveness considerations). Consistent with this notion, effective altruism scholars propose
decision-making frameworks for judging how effective one’s giving will be such as “How many people
benefit, and by how much?” and “What are the chances of success?”7-9 Although earlier critiques
positioned empathy and effectiveness as competing motives, recent evidence suggests they may be
mutually reinforcing, particularly when empathic concern is broadened to include distant others and is
guided by reasoning about impact.10-13

To assess research on the association between charitable giving, effectiveness, and empathy, a
key distinction lies between studies that rely on self-reports of these constructs and studies that
experimentally manipulated them. While the debate about the role of empathy in charitable giving has
gained increasing attention in recent years, prior syntheses have excluded experimental designs, making
this comparison unclear. When it comes to effectiveness, this distinction becomes especially salient
given high-profile experiments suggesting that donors have relatively little appetite to seek out
information about welfare impact14, and that when it is provided effectiveness information has limited
impact on charitable giving15 and choice of charities16.

The goal of this paper is to add an important missing piece to the debate: meta-analyses of the
extent to which charitable responses are, in fact, associated with empathy and perceived effectiveness.
By combining the voices of thousands of participants sampled by hundreds of researchers across several
decades, one is in a stronger position to distinguish signal from noise when examining the associations
between charitable giving, empathy, and effectiveness. We emphasise that the goal of this paper is not
to compare empathy and effectiveness directly. There are too few studies that measure both constructs
within the same sample, and the fields from which these constructs originate use different
operationalisations. Instead, our aim is to provide a descriptive and independent synthesis of the extent
to which each construct is associated with charitable giving, and under what conditions.

Before doing so, some definitional clarification is required. Empathy is a multi-dimensional
construct, one that is often used interchangeably with constructs such as sympathy and compassion. A
particularly important distinction is made between “emotional empathy”, which Bloom refers to as
“feeling what you believe other people feel – experiencing what they experience” (p.3)3 and “cognitive
empathy”, which is variously referred to in the literature as social intelligence, theory of mind, and
perspective taking. In Against Empathy, Bloom makes it clear that his case is primarily about the limits
of affective empathy. So although we meta-analyse all operationalisations of empathy here, we note that
it is affective empathy that is most closely aligned to the debate that inspired the current paper. As
illustrated below, empathy has been operationalised in many different ways (e.g., cognitive versus
affective; dispositional versus situational; experimentally versus correlationally) and drilling down into
the patterns for each helps illuminate the different ways in which empathy may be associated with
charitable giving. Empirical synthesis is overdue: the first meta-analysis on the link between empathy
and prosocial behaviour was published nearly 40 years ago, and incorporated only a handful of studies
on charitable giving.17 Subsequent syntheses have not examined experimental work, focusing
exclusively on correlational links between measures of empathy and questionnaire measures of
dispositional pro-social behaviour18,19 or between measures of empathy and resource allocations in lab-
based games such as the Dictator Game and the Prison er’s Dilemma20.

In extracting data for the effectiveness meta-analysis, we excluded the related literature on
efficiency, that is, the proportion of money that goes to beneficiaries as opposed to being absorbed by
administrative costs.21,22 We made this decision in line with the arguments of effective altruism
advocates, who make it clear that the efficiency of a charity should not be a primary criterion for
judging whether it is effective (i.e., a charity for which 99.99% of income is funnelled directly towards a
pointless mission is efficient but not effective)7. Instead, we meta-analyse studies that measure or
manipulate variables sometimes referred to as “response efficacy”, “perceived donation efficacy”, or
“perceived impact of donation”: constructs that are measured through items such as “How much good
do you think you can do by donating money to this organisation?” or “To what extent do you think that
your donation would make a positive difference?”

Finally, we restricted our analysis to charitable giving, as distinct from other forms of prosocial
behaviour. We defined charitable giving as “voluntary contributions of money that benefit people
outside the giver’s family”.1 We had two reasons for restricting the analysis to charitable giving. First, it
is an operationalisation of giving that most closely aligns to the effective altruism movement, which is
best known for providing moral context around which charities to support financially. Second, by
restricting the range to one domain of prosocial behaviour, we reduce statistical noise and unwanted
heterogeneity associated with comparing effect sizes across different behaviours.23 Patterns of altruism
across domains (e.g., donating money versus blood versus time) are psychologically distinct24, so
focusing just on charitable giving leaves us in a better position to make like-for-like comparisons
between studies.

Here, we show through two meta-analyses that empathy is a robust correlate of charitable giving
and reliably increases generosity when experimentally evoked. Perceived effectiveness, on the other,
hand predicts giving strongly at the self-report level and weakly under experimental manipulation. We
conclude that people give like empathic altruists even when they see themselves as effective ones, a
pattern that sharpens the empirical context within which debates about effective altruism unfold.

---

## Results

We followed the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-analyses
(PRISMA)25,26 to identify quantitative research on (1) the association between effectiveness and
charitable giving and (2) the association between empathy and charitable giving. PRISMA flowcharts,
summarising the screening process, are presented in Supplementary Figs. S1 and S2. Full reference lists
for papers included in the empathy and effectiveness meta-analyses are included in the Supplementary
file.

Pearson’s correlation (r) was used to represent the association between charitable giving and the
two variables of interest: effectiveness and empathy. To approximate a normal sampling distribution,
Pearson r correlations were transformed to Fisher’s z correlations for analyses. For ease of
interpretation, we report values transformed back to Pearson r correlations. Given that the majority of
articles included in both meta-analyses reported multiple dependent effect sizes, we employed a three-
level meta-analytic approach to calculate the overall effect size and perform moderator analyses. All
tests of significance are 2-tailed unless otherwise specified.

We examined publication bias in two ways: visual inspection of the Funnel Plots (where
asymmetry may indicate publication bias) and Egger’s Sandwich test, which was used given the
presence of dependent effect sizes. As can be seen in Fig. 1, no clear or systematic asymmetry is shown
for either meta-analysis. Consistent with visual inspection, Egger’s tests were non-significant for both
effectiveness (p = .260) and empathy (p = .804), indicating no statistical evidence of a pattern indicating
publication bias.

Heterogeneity and treatment of moderators.

We calculated I2 (the proportion of total variance in study results due to heterogeneity rather
than sampling error) which suggested a high degree of heterogeneity for both the effectiveness (96%)
and empathy (92%) meta-analysis. To determine if the within-paper variance (Level 2) and between-
paper variance (Level 3) were significant, two one-tailed log-likelihood-ratio tests were performed.
These tests compared the fit of the three-level model (which accounted for variance at Levels 2 and 3) to
the fit of a two-level model in which variance at only one of the levels was freely estimated. Significant
variance in effect sizes was observed at both the within-paper level (both ps < .001) and between-paper
level (both ps < .001). Using Cheung’s27 formula, 2.48% of the total variance in the association between
effectiveness and charitable giving, and 5.46% of the variance in the association between empathy and
charitable giving, was attributed to sampling variance. Considerably more variance is attributable to
within-paper variance (32.33% in the effectiveness analysis, 24.11% in the empathy meta-analysis) and
between-paper variance (65.19% for effectiveness, 70.43% for empathy). In addition to estimating the
overall effect size, we calculated the prediction interval for each meta-analysis. Prediction intervals
estimate the likely range of effect sizes that might be observed in future studies with similar
characteristics. The range of effect sizes was r = -.17 to r = .71 for effectiveness and r = -.14 and r = .57
for empathy. These heterogeneity tests indicate that the true effects vary significantly across papers and
measures, and that future studies on these associations may report correlations that vary widely.

Moderation analyses identify likely causes of this heterogeneity. To account for the potential
issue of multicollinearity, we followed Hox and colleagues’ recommendation to first test for the effect
of each potential moderator separately using univariate models.28 We then conducted multiple
moderator analyses on a single model that included all significant moderators identified in the univariate
analyses for each meta-analysis.

In the main body of this manuscript, we discuss moderators that are most relevant from a
theoretical and/or practical perspective. For the sake of thoroughness, however, we also ran ancillary
moderation analyses based on sample characteristics: the proportion of women in the sample; the
average age of participants; whether data were collected in Western, Educated, Industrialised, Rich, and
Democratic (WEIRD) or non-WEIRD countries29; whether the sample comprised students or non-
students; and whether the sample was collected using online or offline methods. These analyses are
reported in the bottom half of Tables 1 and 2. In short, none of these sampling characteristics were
statistically significant moderators of the association between effectiveness and charitable giving (all ps
> .35) or the association between empathy and charitable giving (all ps > .08) and so we do not
elaborate on these analyses further.

Effectiveness

Overall, a medium-sized positive association was found between effectiveness and charitable
giving, r = .34, p < .001, t = 9.85, 95% CIs[.28, .40]. However, as can be seen in Table 1, three
moderators significantly qualified this conclusion. First, the association was significantly stronger when
charitable giving was self-reported (e.g., willingness to donate, future intentions to donate, self-reported
past giving; r = .38, p < .001) than when studies used behavioural measures of giving (e.g., direct
observations of giving in the field, the amount of a study payment that the participant donated; r = .27, p
< .001). Second, the association was significantly stronger when participants reported their likelihood of
giving (r = .37, p < .001) compared to when participants reported a monetary value of giving (r = .29, p
< .001). Third, the association between effectiveness and charitable giving was only significant when
effectiveness was measured (r = .42, p < .001). When effectiveness was manipulated, the average effect
was trivial in size and statistically non-significant (r = .03, p = .612).

Finally, we examined whether the different operationalisations of effectiveness corresponded to
differences in strength of association. In the literature, the dominant operationalisation was what we
refer to here as donation effectiveness, a construct that is sometimes referred to as “response efficacy”,
“perceived donation efficacy”, or “perceived impact of donation”. What unites these operationalisations
is that they refer to the extent that the donation will be effective in achieving positive outcomes
(example item: “How much good do you think you can do by donating money to this organisation?”).
However, as can be seen in Table 1, at least three other operationalisations exist in the literature. What
we label as charity effectiveness refers to perceptions of the effectiveness of charities in general
(measured by items such as "Charitable organisations have been quite successful in helping the needy").
What we label as collective effectiveness refers to perceptions of the extent to which collectives can
make a difference (e.g., “I think together we can successfully change things in relation to this issue”)
whereas personal effectiveness refers to perceptions of whether participants can personally make a
difference (e.g., “I think it seems possible to make a big difference"). Regardless of how effectiveness
was operationalised, a significant and positive association was found, the strength of which did not
differ reliably across dimensions.

Following Hox and colleagues’ recommendations28, we extended the three-level meta-regression
model to simultaneously include the moderators identified to be significant in the univariate analyses
(i.e., measured vs manipulated, self-report vs behaviour, likelihood vs value). The multiple moderator
analysis was significant, F(3,150) = 15.51, p < .001, revealing a significant unique moderating effect of
measured vs manipulated effectiveness on the overall association between effectiveness and giving (see
Table 3 for number of effect sizes and statistical output).

Consistent with the univariate analyses, when effects of the other significant moderators were
taken into account, the association between effectiveness and charitable giving was again only
significant when effectiveness was measured (and not when effectiveness was manipulated). However,
the other moderators (self-report vs behaviour, likelihood vs value) were no longer significant. A
possible explanation is that these variables covaried with the measured versus manipulated distinction.
Specifically, experimental studies were more likely to employ behavioural outcomes (rather than self-
reports) and assess donation value (rather than likelihood), which may have suppressed the independent
contributions of these moderators in the full model. In this context, the available data make it difficult to
completely disentangle their unique effects within the multivariate analysis.

Empathy

Overall, a medium-sized positive association was found between empathy and charitable giving,
r = .25, p < .001, t = 11.55, 95% CIs[.21, .29]. Contrary to the pattern of the effectiveness meta-analysis,
there was no statistically significant difference in the strength of that association depending on whether
empathy was measured or manipulated (both rs = .25, both ps < .001; see Table 2). As in the
effectiveness meta-analysis, the association between empathy and charitable giving was significantly
stronger when giving was self-reported (r = .27, p < .001) than when studies used behavioural measures
of giving (r = .22, p < .001). The association was also significantly stronger when giving was measured
in terms of likelihood of giving (r = .29, p < .001) versus the monetary value that participants gave
(r=.21, p<.001). Moreover, a stronger association was found when empathy was operationalised
situationally (i.e., as a state variable; r = .27, p < .001) than when it was measured dispositionally (i.e.,
as a trait variable; r = .20, p < .001).

A final moderator was the dimension of empathy that was being captured. A common critique of
the field is that researchers’ use of the term “empathy” glosses over theoretically meaningful
distinctions. In our systematic review, the dominant operationalisation was what we label here as
emotional empathy, incorporating constructs united by a focus on emotion felt toward a group or
individual in need (variously described in the literature as “compassion”, “sympathy”, “empathic
concern”, or “affective empathy”). As can be seen in Table 2, the strongest association between
empathy and charitable giving emerged when empathy was operationalised this way (r = .27, p < .001).
Significantly weaker than this (but still significant; r = .20, p < .001) were effect sizes in studies in
which empathy was operationalised in a more cognitive way (e.g., as a form of perspective taking
toward a group or individual in need but without any reference to emotion). Finally, some studies
measured empathy as personal distress without explicitly linking that distress to a target group. Most of
these were drawn from studies using the personal distress sub-factor of the Interpersonal Reactivity
Index, which incorporates items such as “Being in a tense emotional situation scares me”.30 When
operationalised this way, empathy shared a relatively small association with charitable giving (r = .09, p
= .005), significantly weaker than for the other two dimensions.

We extended the three-level meta-regression model to simultaneously include the moderators
identified to be significant in the univariate analyses (i.e., state vs trait, dimension of empathy, self-
report vs behaviour, likelihood vs value). The multiple moderator analysis was significant, F(5,228) =
20.15, p < .001, revealing a significant unique moderating effect of state vs trait empathy, dimension of
empathy, and likelihood vs value on the overall association between empathy and giving (see Table 4
for number of effect sizes and statistical output).

When effects of the other significant moderators were accounted for, studies that measured state
empathy yielded a significantly stronger relation compared to studies that measured trait empathy.
Similarly, an identical pattern of findings to the univariate analyses emerged for the dimension of
empathy and likelihood vs value moderators: studies that measured emotional empathy and cognitive
empathy yielded a significantly stronger association than those that measured personal distress, and
studies that captured giving likelihood yielded a significantly stronger association compared to those
that captured giving value. In this model, however, the self-report vs behaviour moderator was no longer
significant.

---

## Methods

Search strategy

Literature searches were initially run in November 2019 and the search was refreshed in
December 2022. The search was conducted across four databases: the two largest multidisciplinary
academic databases (Scopus and Web of Science) plus content-relevant databases in business
(ABI/Inform) and psychology (PsycINFO). For both libraries we used search terms nested around
charitable giving (donation*, donate, donor*, philanthrop*, charitable, "not for profit*", "non profit*",
nonprofit*, NGO*, "non governmental", “third sector” , "charit*") and the factor of interest:
effectiveness (“effective altruism”, “effective giving”, "donation effective*”, “charity effective*”,
“nonprofit effective*”, efficacy, competence, "impact of gift", "donation impact", “nonprofit impact”,
“charity impact”), and empathy (empath*, sympath*, compassion*). Searches were based on title,
abstract, and keywords. Results were supplemented through snowballing from reference lists and open
calls for unpublished data distributed through X and mailing lists of the Association for Research on
Nonprofit Organizations and Voluntary Action, American Marketing Association, and Society for
Personality and Social Psychology. To help identify relevant grey literature, we also screened the first
20 pages (200 results) in Google Scholar (consistent with standard practice)42 using the same search
terms identified in the database searching.

Inclusion criteria and screening

To be eligible for inclusion, studies needed to include a quantitative measure of charitable giving
(as part of correlational or experimental designs), be reported in English, and published 1980 or later.
Correlational studies allowed us to estimate the strength of naturalistic associations, while experimental
studies enabled us to examine causal effects of manipulating empathy or effectiveness on giving
behaviour. We excluded purely qualitative, theoretical, or descriptive studies because they do not
provide effect sizes or statistical associations necessary for meta-analysis. Similarly, we did not include
studies based on simulation models, ethnographic observation, or administrative records without direct
measurement of the psychological constructs of interest, as these designs do not allow for computation
of comparable quantitative associations.

In these meta-analyses, we coded for several moderators. In doing so, we defined intention
likelihood as a self-reported assessment of the likelihood or willingness to donate to a charitable cause
(e.g., “How likely are you to donate to this organisation?”). Value was defined as the monetary value
participants reported they would donate or actually donated. We distinguished between measured
giving, where donation behaviours or intentions were assessed without experimental manipulation of the
constructs of interest, and manipulated giving, where donation behaviours or intentions were measured
after an experimental manipulation aimed at influencing empathy or perceived effectiveness. Self-report
measures refer to participants’ stated responses to survey items about their donation intentions or
behaviour (e.g., likelihood of donating or intended donation amount), whereas behavioural measures
involve participants making actual donation decisions, typically involving real or incentivised financial
contributions.

There were no limits on age or nationality of participants. Papers that were not full-length
articles (e.g., book reviews, books, conference abstracts, corrections, legal judgements) were not
included. The second and third authors screened texts for eligibility on title and then again on abstract,
resolving discrepancies through discussion. Both screeners had experience conducting and publishing
meta-analyses previously. Screening on the full text was conducted by the second author. For articles
less than 10 years old that did not report bivariate effect sizes, we emailed authors to request this
information.

Analytic strategy

Following the screening process, data on the association between effectiveness and charitable
giving were analysed from 47 papers, comprising 81 independent samples and 157 effect sizes (N =
32,116). Data on the association between empathy and charitable giving were analysed from 77 papers,
comprising 105 independent samples and 259 effect sizes (N = 42,681). Where an experiment both
manipulated and measured effectiveness (for example as a manipulation check) both effect sizes were
included (one in the “manipulated” category and one in the “measured” category).

We employed a three-level meta-analytic approach to calculate the overall effect size and
perform moderator analyses. To determine the appropriate level at which to model statistical
dependence among effect sizes, we compared alternative multilevel random-effects structures and
modelled dependence at the paper level; model comparisons and sensitivity analyses are reported in the
OSF supplement. The total variance is partitioned into three components: sampling variance (Level 1),
within-paper variance reflecting dependence among studies in the same article (Level 2), and between-
paper variance (Level 3), thereby appropriately accounting for the clustering of effect sizes. To conduct
our analyses, we followed the procedures outlined by Assink and Wibbelink43 and used the rma.mv
function of the Metafor package44 in the R environment (version 4.4.0)45. We used a multilevel random
effects model, and restricted maximum likelihood estimation method to calculate all model parameters.
The t-distribution was used to test individual regression coefficients and for calculating confidence
intervals46.

The type of bivariate effect size extracted depended on study design, but we typically extracted
Pearson’s correlation coefficients (r) for correlational studies or Cohen’s ds for experimental studies. In
situations where these values were not provided by the study, we used test statistics (e.g., means and
standard deviations, F-values, frequency data) to calculate effect sizes. All effect sizes were transformed
to Pearson r correlations for the meta-analysis (see OSF for effect size conversion formulas).

A leave-one-out analysis did not identify any studies that influenced the overall findings. To
check for extreme effect sizes that may disproportionately influence the results, we screened for those
with standardised scores larger than 3.29 or smaller than 3.29.47 No outliers were identified in the
effectiveness meta-analysis, and only one outlier was identified in the empathy meta-analysis.
Regardless of whether this effect size was included or excluded, analyses yielded similar findings, so we
opted to include this effect size in all subsequent analyses.

Data availability statement

The data are publicly available on the Open Science Framework:
https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/QZ9AX. 48

Code availability statement

Analyses were conducted through R, using code that is viewable on the Open Science Framework:
https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/QZ9AX. 48
